summary:
The Philippines does not criminalise same-sex relations or transgender identity, and same-sex relations have never been criminalised. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. Public sexual conduct or displays of affection can be prosecuted under Article 200 of the Revised Penal Code on Grave Scandal, which carries arresto mayor and public censure for highly scandalous conduct not covered by another article.

A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall, 62 for trans travellers, which falls in the 'Exercise Caution' band, and 81 for HIV-positive travellers.

No administrative legal gender recognition process exists. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. The only affirmed exception is a marker change granted on intersex status. A bill drafted with trans Filipinos would let applicants, including consenting minors, choose markers beyond male and female, such as X or nonbinary; its drafter, Chase Go, links the absence of a recognition process to social exclusion, privacy invasion and violence. Allies planned to endorse the bill to the 20th Congress on 28 July.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination law exists. The SOGIESC Equality Bill has been before Congress for 25 years: it passed the House 198-0 on 20 September 2017, died in the Senate in June 2019, was reintroduced in July 2019, and was rejected by the government in November 2022 as unacceptable. Protection instead comes from a patchwork. Nine provinces prohibit SOGI discrimination, Aklan (2025), Albay (2022), Agusan del Norte (2014), Bataan (2021), Batangas (2015), Cavite (2014-18, with gender identity added in 2018), Dinagat Islands (2016), Ilocos Sur (2017) and Iloilo (2016), alongside ordinances in 32 cities and municipalities. The Magna Carta for Public Social Workers penalises SOGIE harassment with a fine of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment. The Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act punish transphobic, homophobic and misogynistic slurs and ridicule with fines of 1,000 to 10,000 pesos, up to 30 days, and a sensitivity seminar. Republic Act 11166 prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and the 2013 Anti-Bullying Law's implementing rules list sexual orientation and gender identity as prohibited bullying grounds.

Local ordinances restrict gender expression. Marawi City's December 2004 ordinance bans men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings, and also bans skintight blue jeans and tube tops; the mayor described it as part of an Islamic 'cleaning and cleansing' drive. Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence.

Two killings in June 2025 drew national attention: 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol was found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June after being reported missing, and a trans woman former journalist and activist was shot by an unidentified gunman inside a General Santos clinic the same day. Bahaghari cited both as an urgent reason to pass the SOGIESC Equality Bill. Murders of transgender and gender-nonconforming people have been reported from at least 2012, including killings by pro-ISIS groups in Marawi, and after the five-month siege of Marawi some residents blamed the city's LGBTQ community for the militias' wrath while individuals perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps. In May 2025 a foreigner was arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas. On 6 April 2024 drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd at Bayambang, Pangasinan's Kalutan Concert; she called the attack traumatic and the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community. The Commission on Human Rights has called the year's trans killings a 'disturbing pattern of transfemicide'. These are raw counts; no per-capita denominator is published, so they do not establish a rate.

Detention conditions place trans women in male facilities. At Manila City Jail, transgender women and gay men are held in the ordinary male dormitories, where head-shaving on arrival is mandatory, and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy; informal same-sex 'weddings' with male inmates are widely used by gangs as a survival and protection strategy against abuse. BJMP-Davao relocates LGBT detainees in batches to the Davao City Jail Annex 'to prevent abuse', alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, with three LGBT groupings living in the annex since its establishment.

Police have arrested Pride participants. On 26 June 2020 in Manila, police arrested at least 20 participants in an LGBT Pride protest where there were no allegations of violence and participants wore masks and followed social-distancing protocols, subsequently charging them under the 2019 Law on Reporting of Communicable Diseases and the 1985 Public Assembly Act.

Same-sex unions are not recognised as marriage or civil unions; the Family Code recognises only marriages between 'a man and a woman', while the Constitution is silent. House Bill 1015, the Civil Partnership Act, and Senate Bill 449, the Civil Unions Act, seek recognition, benefits and protection. Same-sex couples may not file for joint adoption because their unions are unrecognised, though no explicit law bars LGBTQ+ individuals from adopting and eligibility requirements do not consider sexual orientation or gender identity; adopters may still be deemed unfit for lacking 'good moral character', a term the Civil Code, Family Code and Child and Youth Welfare Code leave open to state interpretation. In June 2023 Quezon City launched the country's first Right to Care Card, letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other through a special power of attorney, rolling out first to government-owned hospitals.
tangentialFactors:
Openly gay and bisexual people have been allowed in the armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017; the uniform policy follows the legal gender recorded on the birth certificate, so a trans service member's documentation governs their treatment.

The Code of Professional Responsibility was updated in 2023 to bar SOGI-based discrimination against clients by lawyers.

In 2025 the Supreme Court ruled that concealment of one's homosexuality from a spouse constituted fraud and a valid basis for annulment of marriage.

School policy has moved ahead of national anti-discrimination law. In late 2016 the Department of Social Welfare and Development and the Department of Education allowed students to wear uniforms matching their gender identity, and the July 2017 Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy requires public school curricula to be reviewed for all gender stereotypes, including LGBTQ-based ones, and mandates observance of June as Pride Month. A 2017 Human Rights Watch report, 'Just Let Us Be', documented bullying and discrimination against LGBT students across Philippine schools and found the law short on remedies at the time; it includes a Tagalog summary and recommendations.

Since the 2000s organisations have formed around sexual health, particularly HIV, psychosocial support and spiritual needs, and counselling and therapy sessions are used to help people leave dangerous and hostile environments.
localsOnly:
Hate crimes and forced conversion therapy have been carried out by family members against Iglesia ni Cristo LGBTQ teenagers, backed by the church's central establishment.

Executive Order No. 51 of 22 December 2023 established the Special Committee on Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Queer, Intersex and Asexual Affairs. Geraldine Roman was elected to Congress in 2016 as the first openly transgender woman to sit there.

Provincial and municipal SOGIE ordinances are the operative protection for most residents outside the national statutes, and their coverage varies by locality; the nine provinces and 32 cities and municipalities listed above are the documented extent.

Residents in Marawi and Kabacan live under the local ordinances described above, which regulate dress and, in Kabacan's case, homosexual relations for Muslims under threat of imprisonment.
outOfScopeNotes:
No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute exists, and the fate of the SOGIESC Equality Bill in the 20th Congress is unresolved.

Enforcement of the Marawi City and Kabacan ordinances is not documented in the sources beyond the text of the ordinances themselves.

The methodology and sample behind the 2026 travel-risk scores are not published.

Sources differ on the number of provinces with SOGIE ordinances: one names eight, another nine, the additional province being Aklan in 2025.

No per-capita denominator accompanies the reported killings of trans people, so no rate can be derived from them.

Whether the Davao City Jail annex practice of segregating LGBT detainees applies in other facilities is not sourced.
